body:
### Problem

We can't change the underlying values by modifying the string keys (`row`/`col`/`start_row`/`start_col`/`end_row`/`end_col`). This changes the string key itself rather than the value it is supposed to modify.

If this behavior is intentional, I would suggest printing a warning and ignoring the assignment when a string key is used.

### Steps to reproduce

```
nvim --clean
```

```lua
local pos = vim.pos(0, 0, 0)
pos.row = 1000
pos.col = 1000

vim.print(pos.row, pos.col) -- 1000; 1000
vim.print(pos[1], pos[2]) -- 0; 0
```

### Expected behavior

I would expect both notations to be interchangeable.

### Nvim version (nvim -v)

NVIM v0.13.0-dev-1278+g0faf4aca73

### Vim (not Nvim) behaves the same?

no

### Operating system/version

Arch Btw

### Terminal name/version

alacritty 0.17.0 (94e7c887)

### $TERM environment variable

tmux-256color, alacritty

### Installation

build from repo

comment_data.body: I can implement this, although we will need a decision on whether assignment should be rejected with an error or allowed.

I can work on this. My proposed approach is to add __newindex to vim.Pos and vim.Range, redirecting assignments to the corresponding numeric fields, with functional tests covering both access forms. Should buf be included as well, or should only the coordinate fields be writable?
There was some discussion about whether the "friendly" keys are needed at all. If the code cost keeps increasing then maybe we should drop them entirely.

> There was some discussion about whether the "friendly" keys are needed at all. If the code cost keeps increasing then maybe we should drop them entirely.

These "friendly" keys are the public API; `pos[1]`, `pos[2]`, and `pos[3]` are an implementation detail (I believe it's like this for optimization?). I suppose we could change the API to make these numeric keys public, but I think it's much better for them to be named.

~~I think the numeric keys are mainly used to make `unpack` work and avoid relying on key strings that may change.~~

I believe the maintenance burden is low enough. Using `.key` with a table feels more natural and provides conventional names for accessing fields, which is actually quite nice. Otherwise, we would either have to use poorly readable `range[1]`, `range[4]`, etc., or create custom variables and worry about naming and redefining them when using multiple positions or ranges close to each other.

The return type of `vim.fn.getregionpos()` still gives me Vietnam flashbacks:

https://github.com/neovim/neovim/blob/a0dc3f00675f738c6e69b71aa7c6e25a99bc4b6f/runtime/doc/lua.txt#L3873-L3883

A few downsides: two syntaxes, creates a naming convention, and makes the code slightly less visually aligned.

As a side note, I can also imagine having a few other getters, such as `pos.row1` and `pos.col1` for 1-based positions.

P.S. Not a proposal, just a point about getters.

I didn't intend to keep `vim.Pos` immutable. In fact, I was planning to make `vim.Pos` support addition and subtraction so that we could expose `to_exclusive_pos` to users. This issue can be fixed directly.
Great, I'll write the fix in the morning.

Slightly off-topic, but loosely related:

```lua
local row, col, buf = unpack(vim.pos(0, 1, 1))
```

Shouldn't it instead be:

```lua
local buf, row, col = unpack(vim.pos(0, 1, 1))
```
```lua
local _, row, col = unpack(vim.pos(0, 1, 1))
```

Can be used for cloning:

```lua
vim.pos(unpack(vim.pos(0, 1, 1)))
```

I think it would be better to use this order, especially since the returned value has string keys as well.
No need to discuss this—it's unsupported behavior. We don't expose numeric keys in the public API, so `unpack` isn't supported.

> `pos[1]`, `pos[2]`, and `pos[3]` are an implementation detail (I believe it's like this for optimization?)

They are not merely an implementation detail. This is signaling to me that people aren't referencing the previous discussions...

Since `lua-language-server` doesn't report any warnings for numeric keys, they aren't de facto private.

From https://github.com/neovim/neovim/pull/41318#issuecomment-5327507896, the main blocker seems to be benchmarking `__newindex`, which can apparently be slow according to Google results.

> No need to discuss this—it's unsupported behavior. We don't expose numeric keys in the public API, so `unpack` isn't supported.

Why? The example in https://github.com/neovim/neovim/issues/41276#issuecomment-5301530426 looks useful and intuitive. And I don't recall any decision about the numeric keys being "private". In fact the opposite, the human-readable fields are only a nice-to-have.

The earliest version I wrote only used string keys like `row` and `col`, but the internal implementation was later changed to use numeric indices for performance, and they are indeed currently marked as private.

https://github.com/neovim/neovim/blob/53cbf66bd2b0d6963ab024733522ab97507af303/runtime/lua/vim/pos.lua#L38-L39

For the same reason, I did not use `unpack()` in the current code. Another reason is that it isn't actually very practical, because for a `vim.Pos`, we can achieve the same effect using `to_extmark()`. e.g.:
```lua
local start_row, start_col, end_row, end_col = range:to_extmark()
```

If we decided to expose these numeric keys, we would be essentially guaranteeing the order of these parameters, which introduces new problems. For instance, as mentioned above, should a parameter like `buf` be placed before or after `row` and `col`? And what should be done if a new parameter, such as `data`, is added?

> should a parameter like `buf` be placed before or after `row` and `col`

it's always the first item. this was settled when we added the buf arg in the `vim.pos` functions.



> we would be essentially guaranteeing the order of these parameters

that's a good thing :)

> I don't recall any decision about the numeric keys being "private".

They are private, at least as for the docs are concerned (undocumented == private).
yes, but that was some "drift" that happened at some point and I didn't notice
